title: Definition
body_md: A locally small category ${\sf C}$ is \emph{locally finitely presentable} (\emph{lfp}, for short) if it is cocomplete and admits a set $\sf G$ of finitely presentable objects such that every object of ${\sf C}$ is a directed colimit of objects from $\sf G$.

title: Caveat
body_md:
In universal algebra, it is customary to consider injective and surjective homomorphisms between algebras of a given class ${\sf K}$. If we regard the latter as a category, with arrows the homomorphisms, the notions of ``surjective'' and ``injective'' are external, as they refer to the forgetful functor to the category of sets. If ${\sf K}$ is a variety or a quasivariety of algebras, then the injective (respectively, surjective) homomorphisms between ${\sf K}$-algebras coincide with the monomorphisms (respectively, regular epimorphisms or, equivalently, extremal epimorphisms) in ${\sf K}$. However, this need not be the case for an arbitrary class of algebras. 

Thus, the categorical formulations of the definability-type properties given above may differ from those in the universal algebra literature when ${\sf K}$ is not a quasivariety. A similar warning applies to the amalgamation-type properties in Section~\ref{s:preliminaries-amalgamation}.

label: d:AP-SAP-IPA
title: Definition
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md: Assume that ${\sf C}$ admits pushouts of spans of monomorphisms. Then ${\sf C}$ has AP if, and only if, monomorphisms are stable under pushouts along monomorphisms. Furthermore, ${\sf C}$ has SAP if, and only if, it has AP and every pushout square consisting entirely of monomorphisms is also a pullback square.

label: l:IPA-iff-SES
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{l:IPA-iff-SES}
Let ${\sf C}$ be any category. Then $\textnormal{IPA}\Rightarrow \textnormal{SES}$, and the converse implication holds if ${\sf C}$ admits cokernel pairs of monomorphisms.

label: d:orthogonal
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{d:orthogonal}
Let $f\colon X\to Y$ be an arrow in a category ${\sf C}$. An object $A$ of ${\sf C}$ is \emph{injective with respect to $f$} if, for every arrow $g\colon X\to A$, there exists an arrow $Y\to A$ making the following diagram commute.
 
\[\begin{tikzcd}
X \arrow{d}[swap]{f} \arrow{r}{g} & A \\
Y \arrow[dashed]{ur} &
\end{tikzcd}\]
 
If the dashed arrows are unique, we say that $A$ is \emph{orthogonal to $f$}.
If $\mathcal{W}$ is a collection of arrows of ${\sf C}$, we say that $A$ is \emph{injective with respect to $\mathcal{W}$} (respectively, \emph{orthogonal to $\mathcal{W}$}) if it is injective with respect to each member of $\mathcal{W}$ (respectively, orthogonal to each member of $\mathcal{W}$).
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md: The uniqueness condition in Definition~\ref{d:orthogonal} is met automatically if $f$ is epic. In this case, $A$ is orthogonal to $f$ just when it is injective with respect to~$f$.
head: environment

title: Definition
body_md: A full subcategory of ${\sf C}$ is a \emph{(small-)orthogonality class} if it is of the form ${\mathcal{W}}^{\perp}$ for a (small) collection of morphisms $\mathcal{W}$ of ${\sf C}$.
head: environment

label: p:localise-epis
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{p:localise-epis}
Let ${\sf C}$ be an lfp category, and let $\mathcal{W}$ be a class of arrows in ${\sf C}$. If each member of $\mathcal{W}$ is an epimorphism, then ${\mathcal{W}}^{\perp}$ is a reflective subcategory of ${\sf C}$.

label: orthog-reflective
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{orthog-reflective}
Suppose that ${\sf C}$ is an lfp category. Every $\omega$-orthogonality class in ${\sf C}$ is a reflective subcategory closed under directed colimits in ${\sf C}$ and, moreover, it is lfp.
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md: The converse of Theorem~\ref{orthog-reflective} is false: not every reflective subcategory of an lfp category ${\sf C}$, closed under directed colimits in ${\sf C}$, is an $\omega$-orthogonality class; see~\cite{Volger1979} for a counterexample. Characterisations of $\omega$-orthogonality classes in lfp categories have been provided in~\cite{HAR2001,AS2004}.
head: environment

label: rm:purity
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rm:purity}
  Let us call an object $X$ \emph{absolutely $\omega$-pure} if every monomorphism with domain $X$ is $\omega$-pure. In the category of $R$-modules, for $R$ any ring, the absolutely $\omega$-pure objects are the absolutely pure modules in the usual sense (see e.g.\ \cite{Maddox1967}). In the category of fields, they are the algebraically closed fields. See~\cite{Rothmaler1997} for a nice survey on this topic. As shown in \cite[Proposition~2.31]{ar94book}, every $\omega$-pure morphism in an lfp category is a regular monomorphism. Therefore, every absolutely $\omega$-pure object in an lfp category is absolutely closed and, a fortiori, saturated.
head: environment

label: t:charact-inj-classes
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{t:charact-inj-classes}
A full subcategory ${\sf D}$ of an lfp category ${\sf C}$ is an $\omega$-injectivity class if, and only if, it is closed in ${\sf C}$ under products, directed colimits, and $\omega$-pure subobjects.

label: p:saturated-Beth-comp-lfp
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{p:saturated-Beth-comp-lfp}
Let ${\sf D}$ be a balanced, full and replete mono-reflective subcategory of an lfp category ${\sf C}$. Then ${\sf D}$ coincides with ${\sf Sat}({\sf C})$.
head: environment

label: l:mono-refl-sat
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{l:mono-refl-sat}
Let ${\sf D}$ be a full, replete and mono-reflective subcategory of a category~${\sf C}$. Then ${\sf D}$ contains ${\sf Sat}({\sf C})$. If, in addition, ${\sf D}$ is balanced and every object of ${\sf C}$ admits an epi-mono to a saturated object, then ${\sf D}$ is contained in ${\sf Sat}({\sf C})$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $R\colon {\sf D}\hookrightarrow {\sf C}$ be the inclusion functor, $L$ its left adjoint, and $\eta$ the unit of the adjunction.
 
For the first part of the statement, observe that the component $\eta_{A}$ of $\eta$ at an object~$A$ of ${\sf C}$ is an epi-mono with domain $A$, hence $\eta_{A}$ is an isomorphism whenever $A$ is saturated. Since ${\sf D}$ is a replete subcategory of ${\sf C}$, it follows that every saturated object of ${\sf C}$ belongs to ${\sf D}$.

For the second part of the statement, it suffices to show that, for each object $A$ of~${\sf C}$, $RL(A)$ belongs to ${\sf Sat}({\sf C})$. Consider an epi-mono $f\colon RL(A)\to E$ with $E$ in ${\sf Sat}({\sf C})$. It follows from the previous part of the proof that $E$ belongs to ${\sf D}$. Thus, since ${\sf D}$ is balanced, $f$ is an isomorphism and so $RL(A)$ belongs to ${\sf Sat}({\sf C})$.
head: environment

label: def:epi-extension
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{def:epi-extension}
An \emph{epi-extension} of $A$ is any epi-mono in ${\sf C}$ with domain $A$. Write $\operatorname{Ext_{p}}(A)$ for the sub-preorder of $\operatorname{Ext}(A)$ consisting of the epi-extensions of $A$. An element $m\in \operatorname{Ext_{p}}(A)$ is \emph{maximal} if, for any $n\in \operatorname{Ext_{p}}(A)$, $m\preccurlyeq n$ implies $m\sim n$.
head: environment

label: rem:order-on-epi-ext
title: Remark
head: environment

label: l:maximal-saturated
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
\ref{i:codomain-saturated} $\Rightarrow$ \ref{i:maximal-in-EExt}. If $n\colon A\rightarrowtail B$ is an epi-extension of $A$ satisfying $m\preccurlyeq n$, by Remark~\ref{rem:order-on-epi-ext}\ref{i:preceq-unique-epi-mono} there is an epi-mono $h\colon E\rightarrowtail B$ such that $n=h\circ m$. As $E$ is saturated, $h$ is an isomorphism. Thus, $m\sim n$ by Remark~\ref{rem:order-on-epi-ext}\ref{i:sym-equi}.

\ref{i:maximal-in-EExt} $\Rightarrow$ \ref{i:codomain-saturated}. Suppose $h\colon E\to B$ is an epi-mono. Since $m\preccurlyeq h\circ m$ in $\operatorname{Ext_{p}}(A)$, and $m$ is maximal, we get $m\sim h\circ m$. Thus, $h$ is an isomorphism by Remark~\ref{rem:order-on-epi-ext}\ref{i:unique-epi-mono-is-iso}.
head: environment

label: l:existence-saturated-epi-ext
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{l:existence-saturated-epi-ext}
In an lfp category, every object admits a saturated epi-extension.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: Let $A$ be an object of an lfp category, and let $P$ be the poset reflection of the preorder $\operatorname{Ext_{p}}(A)$ of epi-extensions of $A$. Further, let $\operatorname{Epi}(A)$ be the poset of subobjects of $A$ regarded as an object of~${\sf C}^{{\mathrm{op}}}$. By item~\ref{i:sym-equi} in Remark~\ref{rem:order-on-epi-ext}, there is an injective map $P\to \operatorname{Epi}(A)$. Since every lfp category is well-copowered \cite[Theorem~1.58]{ar94book}, $\operatorname{Epi}(A)$ is small, and thus so is $P$. Note that $P$ is non-empty because it contains the (equivalence class of) the identity of $A$. Moreover, every chain in $P$ admits an upper bound, which can be obtained by computing the colimit $A_{\omega}$ of the chain. The colimit map $A\to A_{\omega}$ is easily seen to be epic, and it is monic by \cite[Proposition~1.62]{ar94book}. By Zorn's Lemma, there exists a maximal element in $P$. In view of Lemma~\ref{l:maximal-saturated}, such a maximal element is (represented by) an epi-extension $A\to E$ with $E$ saturated.

label: l:basic-props-mono-reflections
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Suppose that $e\colon X\to Y$ is an epimorphism in ${\sf D}$, and consider arrows $f,g\colon R(Y)\rightrightarrows A$ in ${\sf C}$ such that $f\circ R(e) = g\circ R(e)$. Composing with the component of the unit at $A$, i.e.\ $\eta_{A}\colon A\to RL(A)$, we get $\eta_{A}\circ f\circ R(e) = \eta_{A}\circ g\circ R(e)$. Since ${\sf D}$ is a full subcategory of ${\sf C}$, there exist arrows $u,v\colon Y\rightrightarrows L(A)$ in ${\sf D}$ such that $R(u)=\eta_{A}\circ f$ and $R(v)=\eta_{A}\circ g$. It follows that 
\[
R(u\circ e) = R(u)\circ R(e)= R(v)\circ R(e) = R(v\circ e),
\]
and so $u\circ e = v\circ e$ in ${\sf D}$ because $R$ is faithful. As $e$ is an epimorphism, we get $u=v$ and therefore $\eta_{A}\circ f = \eta_{A}\circ g$. Using the fact that $\eta_{A}$ is monic, we conclude that $f=g$, showing that $R(e)$ is epic.

It is straightforward to see that any fully faithful functor that preserves epis must reflect extremal monos. Hence, $R$ reflects extremal monos. 
 
To see that $R$ reflects regular monos, suppose that $f\colon X\to Y$ is an arrow in ${\sf D}$ such that $R(f)$ is the equaliser of a pair of parallel arrows $u,v\colon R(Y)\rightrightarrows A$. 
Composing with the component $\eta_{A}$ of the unit at $A$, we obtain arrows $u'\coloneqq \eta_{A}\circ u$ and $v'\coloneqq \eta_{A}\circ v$. Since $\eta_{A}$ is monic, $R(f)$ is also the equaliser of $u'$ and $v'$. As $R$ is full, there are arrows $g,h\colon Y\rightrightarrows L(A)$ such that $R(g)=u'$ and $R(h)=v'$. Using the fact that fully faithful functors reflect limits, we conclude that $f$ is the equaliser of $g$ and $h$.

Finally, recall that, given an adjoint pair of functors, the left adjoint is faithful if, and only if, the unit of the adjunction is pointwise monic (see e.g.\ \cite[Theorem~19.14(1)]{ahs06book} for the dual statement). Thus, the reflector $L$ is faithful.

label: t:Beth-companion-unique
title: Theorem
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The uniqueness of the Beth companion and the implication \ref{i:has-Beth-comp} $\Rightarrow$ \ref{i:Beth-comp-is-Sigma} are immediate consequences of Proposition~\ref{p:saturated-Beth-comp-lfp}.

\ref{i:Beth-comp-is-Sigma} $\Rightarrow$ \ref{i:Sigma-axiomatisable}. Since ${\sf Sat}({\sf C})$ is a reflective subcategory of an lfp category, it is complete and cocomplete. 
 
The inclusion functor ${\sf Sat}({\sf C})\hookrightarrow{\sf C}$ preserves limits and directed colimits, hence ${\sf Sat}({\sf C})$ is closed under limits and directed colimits in ${\sf C}$.

\ref{i:Sigma-axiomatisable} $\Rightarrow$ \ref{i:has-Beth-comp}. By \cite[Corollary~2.4]{MP1987} (see also \cite[Corollary~2.48]{ar94book}), a full subcategory of an lfp category ${\sf C}$ is itself lfp provided that it is closed in ${\sf C}$ under limits and directed colimits. Hence, ${\sf Sat}({\sf C})$ is lfp and the inclusion functor ${\sf Sat}({\sf C})\hookrightarrow{\sf C}$ is right adjoint by \cite[Theorem~1.66]{ar94book}. As every object of ${\sf C}$ admits a saturated epi-extension by Lemma~\ref{l:existence-saturated-epi-ext}, ${\sf Sat}({\sf C})$ is a (full and replete) mono-reflective subcategory of ${\sf C}$. To conclude that ${\sf Sat}({\sf C})$ is a Beth companion of ${\sf C}$, it remains to show that ${\sf Sat}({\sf C})$ has the \textnormal{ES}~property. In turn, this follows from the fact that the inclusion ${\sf Sat}({\sf C})\hookrightarrow {\sf C}$ reflects extremal monomorphisms by Lemma~\ref{l:basic-props-mono-reflections}.

title: Remark
head: environment

label: rmk:comparison-Beth-companions
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rmk:comparison-Beth-companions}
Let ${\sf K}$ be a quasivariety with the amalgamation property that admits a Beth companion ${\sf M}$ in the sense of \cite{CKM2026bis}; in particular, this means that~${\sf M}$ must also be a quasivariety. Then ${\sf M}$ is a strong Beth companion in our~sense. Indeed, Theorem~2.2 and Corollary~3.2 in \emph{op.~cit.} imply that ${\sf M}$ is (isomorphic to) a mono-reflective subcategory of ${\sf K}$ satisfying \textnormal{SES}. Considering the underlying-set functors $U_{{\sf M}}$ and $U_{{\sf K}}$, we obtain a commutative diagram as follows.
\[\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=1em, row sep=1.5em]
{\sf M} \arrow[hookrightarrow]{rr} \arrow{dr}[swap]{U_{{\sf M}}} & & {\sf K} \arrow{dl}{U_{{\sf K}}} \\
& {\sf Set} &
\end{tikzcd}\]
Since ${\sf K}$ and ${\sf M}$ are quasivarieties, $U_{{\sf M}}$ and $U_{{\sf K}}$ create directed colimits. Therefore, the inclusion ${\sf M}\hookrightarrow {\sf K}$ preserves directed colimits, and so ${\sf M}$ is a strong Beth companion of ${\sf K}$ in our sense.
head: environment

label: t:strong-Beth-companion-unique
title: Theorem
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We already observed that, if they exist, strong Beth companions are unique.

\ref{i:has-strong-Beth-comp} $\Rightarrow$ \ref{i:beth-comp-exists-and-sat-equal-abs}. It suffices to show that ${\sf Sat}({\sf C})\subseteq{\sf Abs}({\sf C})$, since the converse is always true. Note that, if ${\sf C}$ admits a strong Beth companion, then the latter coincides with ${\sf Sat}({\sf C})$ by Theorem~\ref{t:Beth-companion-unique}. Thus, ${\sf Sat}({\sf C})$ is a strong Beth companion of~${\sf C}$.

Let $X$ be a saturated object of ${\sf C}$, and let $m\colon X\rightarrowtail Y$ be a mono in ${\sf C}$. Since ${\sf Sat}({\sf C})$ is a  mono-reflective subcategory of ${\sf C}$, composing $m$ with the component $\eta_{Y}\colon Y \rightarrowtail Y^{*}$ of the unit at $Y$, we obtain a monomorphism $g\coloneqq \eta_{Y}\circ m \colon X\rightarrowtail Y^{*}$ in ${\sf C}$ between saturated objects. As ${\sf Sat}({\sf C})$ satisfies \textnormal{SES}, $g$ is a regular mono in ${\sf Sat}({\sf C})$. The inclusion functor ${\sf Sat}({\sf C})\hookrightarrow{\sf C}$ preserves limits because it is right adjoint, so $g$ is a regular monomorphism in ${\sf C}$. Since $\eta_{Y}$ is monic, it follows that $m$ is a regular mono. That is, $X$ is absolutely closed in ${\sf C}$.

\ref{i:beth-comp-exists-and-sat-equal-abs} $\Rightarrow$ \ref{i:abs-is-strong-beth-comp}. By Theorem~\ref{t:Beth-companion-unique}, if ${\sf C}$ admits a Beth companion, then ${\sf Sat}({\sf C})$ is a Beth companion of ${\sf C}$. If ${\sf Sat}({\sf C})={\sf Abs}({\sf C})$, then the latter is also a Beth companion of ${\sf C}$. As observed above, ${\sf Abs}({\sf C})$ is a Beth companion of ${\sf C}$ precisely when it is a strong Beth companion. 

\ref{i:abs-is-strong-beth-comp} $\Rightarrow$ \ref{i:has-strong-Beth-comp}. Clear.

label: d:EAP
title: Definition
head: environment

label: rmk:EAP-unique-saturated-epi-ext
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rmk:EAP-unique-saturated-epi-ext}
Recall from Definition~\ref{def:epi-extension} and Lemma~\ref{l:maximal-saturated} that $\operatorname{Ext_{p}}(A)$ denotes the preorder of epi-extensions of an object $A$, whose maximal elements are the saturated epi-extensions of $A$. Using the fact that every object of an lfp category admits a saturated epi-extension (Lemma~\ref{l:existence-saturated-epi-ext}), it is not difficult to see that an lfp category ${\sf C}$ satisfies \textnormal{EAP}~if, and only if, for every object $A$ of ${\sf C}$, the preorder $\operatorname{Ext_{p}}(A)$ has a top element. In particular, if ${\sf C}$ satisfies \textnormal{EAP}, then each of its objects admits, up to isomorphism, exactly one saturated epi-extension.

label: l:Ringel-restated
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{l:Ringel-restated}
Let ${\sf C}$ be any category satisfying \textnormal{EAP}. For every full mono-reflective subcategory ${\sf D}$ of ${\sf C}$, the reflector ${\sf C} \to {\sf D}$ preserves epi-monos.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We start by proving that \textnormal{EAP}~implies the following 2-out-of-3 property for epi-monos: given a composite arrow $g\circ f$ in ${\sf C}$, if both $g\circ f$ and $f$ are epi-monos, then so is $g$. Clearly, $g$ is always epic. To see that it is monic, note that \textnormal{EAP}~entails the existence of monomorphisms $u,v$ making the following diagram commute.
\[\begin{tikzcd}[cells={nodes={inner sep=2pt, outer sep=1pt}}]
\phantom{\cdot} \arrow{r}{f} \arrow{d}[swap]{g\circ f} & \phantom{\cdot} \arrow[dashed]{d}{u} \\
\phantom{\cdot} \arrow[dashed]{r}{v} & \phantom{\cdot}
\end{tikzcd}\]
 
As $f$ is epic, the equality $u\circ f = v\circ g\circ f$ implies $u= v\circ g$. Since $u$ is monic, so is $g$. 


Now, let $R\colon {\sf D}\hookrightarrow{\sf C}$ be a full mono-reflective subcategory, with reflector $L\colon {\sf C}\to{\sf D}$, and write $\eta$ for the unit of the adjunction $L\dashv R$. For any arrow $f\colon X\to Y$ in ${\sf C}$, there is a naturality square as displayed below.
\[\begin{tikzcd}[cells={nodes={inner sep=2pt, outer sep=1pt}}]
\phantom{\cdot} \arrow{r}{f} \arrow{d}[swap]{\eta_{X}} & \phantom{\cdot} \arrow{d}{\eta_{Y}} \\
\phantom{\cdot} \arrow{r}[swap]{RL(f)} & \phantom{\cdot}
\end{tikzcd}\]
Since ${\sf D}$ is a mono-reflective subcategory of ${\sf C}$, the components of $\eta$ are epi-monic. If~$f$ is an epi-mono, then so is the composite $\eta_{Y}\circ f = RL(f)\circ \eta_{X}$. It follows from the 2-out-of-3 property established above that $RL(f)$ is an epi-mono. The functor~$R$ reflects epi-monos because it is faithful; therefore $L(f)$ is epi-monic.

label: l:equivalent-problems
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $R\colon {\sf D}\hookrightarrow{\sf C}$ be the inclusion functor, $L\colon {\sf C}\to{\sf D}$ the reflector, and $\eta$ the unit of the adjunction $L\dashv R$.

\ref{i:catt-balanced} $\Rightarrow$ \ref{i:inverts-epi-monos}. If $f$ is an epi-mono in ${\sf C}$, then $L(f)$ is an epi-mono in ${\sf D}$ by Lemma~\ref{l:Ringel-restated}. As ${\sf D}$ is balanced, it follows that $L(f)$ is an isomorphism.

title: Lemma

title: Proof

label: p:localisation-is-X-ort
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{p:localisation-is-X-ort}
For any full and replete mono-reflective subcategory ${\sf D}\hookrightarrow {\sf C}$ of an lfp category~${\sf C}$, we have ${\mathcal{X}}^{\perp}\subseteq {\sf D}$. If, in addition, ${\sf C}$ satisfies \textnormal{EAP}~and ${\sf D}$ is balanced, then ${\mathcal{X}}^{\perp}= {\sf D}$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let ${\sf D}\hookrightarrow {\sf C}$ be a mono-reflective subcategory, with reflector $L$. Every full and replete reflective subcategory is the localisation at the collection of arrows inverted by the reflector; thus we can identify ${\sf D}$ with the localisation of ${\sf C}$ at $\mathcal{W}\coloneqq L^{-1}(\text{isos})$. 

The functor $L$ is faithful by Lemma~\ref{l:basic-props-mono-reflections}, so it reflects epis and monos. It follows that $f$ is epi-mono whenever $L(f)$ is an isomorphism. That is, $\mathcal{W}\subseteq \mathcal{X}$.
 
As the reflector ${\sf C} \to {\mathcal{X}}^{\perp}$ inverts all epi-monos, hence all arrows in $\mathcal{W}$, we get ${\mathcal{X}}^{\perp}\subseteq {\sf D}$.

If, in addition, ${\sf C}$ satisfies \textnormal{EAP}~and ${\sf D}$ is balanced, then $\mathcal{X}\subseteq \mathcal{W}$ by Lemma~\ref{l:equivalent-problems}. It follows that ${\mathcal{X}}^{\perp}= {\sf D}$.

label: d:TEM
title: Definition

label: l:ort-vs-sat
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
\ref{i:X-local-extension} $\Leftrightarrow$ \ref{i:sat-and-ort-coincide}. As every object of an lfp category has a saturated (epi-)extension by Lemma~\ref{l:existence-saturated-epi-ext}, the implication \ref{i:sat-and-ort-coincide} $\Rightarrow$ \ref{i:X-local-extension} is immediate. For the converse implication, suppose that every object of ${\sf C}$ admits an extension with codomain in ${\mathcal{X}}^{\perp}$. Then ${\mathcal{X}}^{\perp}$ is a mono-reflective subcategory of ${\sf C}$. The unit of this mono-reflection is component-wise epi-monic, hence its component at any saturated object is an isomorphism. It follows that ${\sf Sat}({\sf C})\subseteq {\mathcal{X}}^{\perp}$, and so ${\sf Sat}({\sf C})={\mathcal{X}}^{\perp}$ by Lemma~\ref{l:ort-included-in-sigma}.

\ref{i:sat-and-ort-coincide} $\Leftrightarrow$ \ref{i:transferable-epi-monos}.
Suppose that ${\mathcal{X}}^{\perp} = {\sf Sat}({\sf C})$. We claim that ${\sf C}$ has transferable epi-monos. Consider an epi-mono $m\colon Y\to W$ and an arrow $f\colon Y\to X$. Since ${\sf C}$ is lfp, $X$ admits a saturated epi-extension $n\colon X\to Z$. As ${\sf Sat}({\sf C})\subseteq {\mathcal{X}}^{\perp}$, there is an arrow $g$ making the following diagram commute. Thus, ${\sf C}$ has transferable epi-monos.
\[\begin{tikzcd}
Y \arrow{d}[swap]{m} \arrow{r}{f} & X \arrow{d}{n} \\
W \arrow[dashed]{r}{g} & Z
\end{tikzcd}\]

Conversely, we claim that if ${\sf C}$ has transferable epi-monos, then ${\mathcal{X}}^{\perp} = {\sf Sat}({\sf C})$ (for this, we do not need to assume that ${\sf C}$ is lfp). 
 
Suppose that $X$ is a saturated object of ${\sf C}$, and consider a span $f,m$ as displayed below, with $m$ epi-mono.
\[\begin{tikzcd}
Y \arrow{d}[swap]{m} \arrow{r}{f} & X \arrow[dashed]{d}{n} \\
W \arrow[dashed]{r}{h} & Z
\end{tikzcd}\]
Since ${\sf C}$ has transferable epi-monos, there exist arrows $h,n$, with $n$ epi-mono, making the above square commute. As $X$ is saturated, $n$ is an isomorphism. Hence, $g\coloneqq n^{-1}\circ h\colon W\to X$ satisfies $g\circ m = f$, showing that $X$ is orthogonal to~$m$. This proves that ${\sf Sat}({\sf C})\subseteq {\mathcal{X}}^{\perp}$; the other inclusion follows from Lemma~\ref{l:ort-included-in-sigma}.

title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rmk:EAP-vs-TEM}
Let ${\sf C}$ be an lfp category satisfying \textnormal{EAP}. It follows from Theorem~\ref{t:Beth-companion-amalgam-orthogonal} and Lemma~\ref{l:ort-vs-sat} that, if ${\sf C}$ has a Beth companion, then it satisfies the strengthening \textnormal{TEM}~of \textnormal{EAP}. In other words, \textnormal{TEM}~and \textnormal{EAP}~are equivalent for any lfp category that admits a Beth companion.

label: l:X-ort-dir-colim-fp-domains
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
\ref{i:ort-X-closed-dir-col} $\Rightarrow$ \ref{i:saturation-epimonos-fp-domains}. Let $A$ be any object of ${\sf C}$, and let $D_{A}$ be the canonical (directed) diagram of finitely presentable objects of ${\sf C}$ satisfying $A\cong \operatornamewithlimits{colim}{D_{A}}$. Recall that ${\mathcal{X}}^{\perp}$ is mono-reflective in ${\sf C}$ by Proposition~\ref{p:localise-epis} and Lemma~\ref{l:ort-vs-sat}. Write $R\colon {\mathcal{X}}^{\perp}\hookrightarrow {\sf C}$ for the inclusion functor, $L$ for its left adjoint, and $\eta$ for the unit of this adjunction. Then $\eta_{A}$ is the colimit, in the category of arrows of ${\sf C}$, of the arrows~$\eta_{B}$, where $B$ ranges over the image of the diagram $D_{A}$. Just observe that colimits in the arrow category are computed componentwise, and both $L$ and $R$ preserve directed colimits. 

The class of arrows inverted by the reflector ${\sf C} \to \mathcal{X}^{\perp}_{\mathrm{fpd}}$ contains each arrow of the form $\eta_{B}$ and is closed under colimits in the arrow category; therefore, it contains all components of the unit $\eta$. It follows that ${\mathcal{X}}^{\perp}$, which can be identified with the localisation at the components of $\eta$, coincides with $\mathcal{X}^{\perp}_{\mathrm{fpd}}$.

\ref{i:saturation-epimonos-fp-domains} $\Rightarrow$ \ref{i:ort-X-closed-dir-col}. Each arrow in $\mathcal{X}_{\mathrm{fpd}}$ is an epimorphism with a finitely presentable domain, hence $\mathcal{X}^{\perp}_{\mathrm{fpd}}$ is closed in ${\sf C}$ under directed colimits (this follows from a straightforward adaptation of \cite[Proposition~1.35]{ar94book}). Thus, so is ${\mathcal{X}}^{\perp}$.

label: cor:Beth-TEM-omega-ort
title: Corollary
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
By Lemma~\ref{l:ort-vs-sat}, we can assume throughout the proof that ${\sf Sat}({\sf C})={\mathcal{X}}^{\perp}$.

\ref{i:TEM-has-BC} $\Rightarrow$ \ref{i:TEM-Sat-dir-col}. This is an immediate consequence of Theorem~\ref{t:Beth-companion-unique}. 

\ref{i:TEM-Sat-dir-col} $\Rightarrow$ \ref{i:TEM-Sat-inj-class}. By Theorem~\ref{t:charact-inj-classes}, it suffices to prove that ${\sf Sat}({\sf C})$ is closed in ${\sf C}$ under $\omega$-pure subobjects; just recall that ${\mathcal{X}}^{\perp}$ is always closed in ${\sf C}$ under limits, and thus so is ${\sf Sat}({\sf C})$. Every $\omega$-pure morphism in an lfp category is a regular monomorphism (see e.g.\ \cite[Proposition~2.31]{ar94book}), hence an extremal monomorphism. Therefore, it is enough to show that the class of saturated objects in ${\sf C}$ is closed under extremal subobjects. Consider an extremal mono $m\colon X \to Y$ in ${\sf C}$, with $Y$ saturated, and let $f\colon X\to W$ be an epi-mono. We must prove that $f$ is an isomorphism. By \textnormal{TEM}, the span formed by $m$ and $f$ can be completed into a commutative square as displayed below, with $g$ epi-monic.
\[\begin{tikzcd}
X \arrow{r}{m} \arrow{d}[swap]{f} & Y \arrow{d}{g} \\
W \arrow{r}{h} & Z
\end{tikzcd}\]
 
Since $Y$ is saturated, $g$ is an isomorphism, and therefore $h\circ f = g\circ m$ is an extremal mono. It follows that $f$ is an extremal mono, hence an isomorphism.


\ref{i:TEM-Sat-inj-class} $\Rightarrow$ \ref{i:TEM-has-BC}. Every $\omega$-injectivity class in ${\sf C}$ is closed under directed colimits in ${\sf C}$ by Theorem~\ref{t:charact-inj-classes}, so ${\sf Sat}({\sf C})={\mathcal{X}}^{\perp}$ is a Beth companion of ${\sf C}$ by Theorem~\ref{t:Beth-companion-amalgam-orthogonal} and Lemma~\ref{l:ort-vs-sat}.

label: cor:S-perp-Beth-comp
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:S-perp-Beth-comp}
Let ${\sf C}$ be an lfp category with transferable epi-monos, and let $\mathcal{S}$ be a class of epi-monos in ${\sf C}$ with finitely presentable domains. If ${\mathcal{S}}^{\perp}$ is balanced, then it is the Beth companion of~${\sf C}$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
If $\mathcal{S}$ is any class of epi-monos between objects of ${\sf C}$, then ${\mathcal{X}}^{\perp}\subseteq {\mathcal{S}}^{\perp}$. By Proposition~\ref{p:localise-epis}, ${\mathcal{S}}^{\perp}$ is a reflective subcategory of ${\sf C}$; in fact, it is mono-reflective because every object of ${\sf C}$ admits an extension with codomain in ${\mathcal{X}}^{\perp}$ (hence, in~${\mathcal{S}}^{\perp}$) by Lemma~\ref{l:ort-vs-sat}.
 
If ${\mathcal{S}}^{\perp}$ is balanced, then ${\mathcal{S}}^{\perp}={\mathcal{X}}^{\perp}$ by Proposition~\ref{p:localisation-is-X-ort}. If, in addition, the domain of each arrow in $\mathcal{S}$ is finitely presentable, then ${\mathcal{S}}^{\perp}$ is closed under directed colimits in ${\sf C}$ (this follows from a straightforward adaptation of \cite[Proposition~1.35]{ar94book}, using the fact that each arrow in $\mathcal{S}$ is an epimorphism). 
 
Therefore, ${\mathcal{S}}^{\perp}$ is the Beth companion of ${\sf C}$ by Theorem~\ref{t:Beth-companion-amalgam-orthogonal} and Corollary~\ref{cor:Beth-TEM-omega-ort}.

label: Hebert
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{Hebert}
  Let ${\sf C}$ be an lfp category satisfying \textnormal{TEM}, and $\mathcal{X}$ the class of epi-monos in ${\sf C}$. Denote by $\mathcal{M}$ the class of arrows in ${\sf C}$ having the \emph{right lifting property} with respect to all arrows in $\mathcal{X}$ (see e.g. \cite[\S 11.1]{Riehl2014}). The following statements hold:
  \begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
    \item\label{i:ortho-X-replete-mono-reflective} ${\mathcal{X}}^{\perp}$ is a full replete mono-reflective subcategory of ${\sf C}$ if, and only if, $(\mathcal{X},\mathcal{M})$ is a factorisation system in ${\sf C}$.
    \item\label{i:Beth-comp-factorisation-system} If $(\mathcal{X},\mathcal{M})$ is a factorisation system in ${\sf C}$ and $\mathcal{M}$ is closed under directed colimits in the category of arrows of ${\sf C}$, then ${\sf C}$ admits a Beth companion.
  \end{enumerate}
 The left-to-right implication in item~\ref{i:ortho-X-replete-mono-reflective} follows from \cite[Corollary~3.4]{CHK1985}, combined with the fact that $\mathcal{X}$ coincides with the class of arrows inverted by the reflector ${\sf C} \to {\mathcal{X}}^{\perp}$. The right-to-left implication follows from the considerations in~\cite[\S 2]{CHK1985}. Item~\ref{i:Beth-comp-factorisation-system} is a consequence of Corollary~\ref{cor:Beth-TEM-omega-ort}, since ${\mathcal{X}}^{\perp}$ is closed under directed colimits in ${\sf C}$ whenever $\mathcal{M}$ is closed under directed colimits in the arrow category.

\label{t:characterisation-quasi-varieties}
A category is equivalent to a finitary (possibly multi-sorted) quasivariety if, and only if, it is cocomplete and admits a dense\footnote{For our purposes, a dense subcategory of a category ${\sf D}$ can be defined as a full subcategory $\sf E$ of ${\sf D}$ such that the restricted Yoneda embedding ${\sf D} \to [\sf{E}^{{\mathrm{op}}},{\sf Set}]$ is fully faithful.} subcategory consisting of finitely presentable regular projectives.

body_md: To characterise mono-sorted quasivarieties, it suffices to require that the dense subcategory in the above statement consists of a single finitely presentable regular projective object.

label: t:transfer-quasi-variety
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{t:transfer-quasi-variety}
Suppose ${\sf C}$ satisfies \textnormal{EAP}, and there is a class $\mathcal{S}$ of epi-monos in ${\sf C}$ with finitely presentable regular projective domains such that ${\mathcal{S}}^{\perp}$ is balanced. If~${\sf C}$ is equivalent to a (mono-sorted) finitary (quasi)variety, then so is its Beth companion.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $\mathcal{S}$ be as in the statement. Upon recalling that ${\sf C}$ satisfies \textnormal{TEM}~(see Remark~\ref{rmk:EAP-vs-TEM}), it follows from Corollary~\ref{cor:S-perp-Beth-comp} that ${\mathcal{S}}^{\perp}$ is the Beth companion of~${\sf C}$. Let $R\colon {\mathcal{S}}^{\perp}\hookrightarrow {\sf C}$ denote the inclusion functor, and $L$ its left adjoint. 

By Theorem~\ref{t:characterisation-quasi-varieties}, it suffices to show that if ${\sf D}$ is a dense subcategory of ${\sf C}$ consisting of finitely presentable regular projectives, then the full subcategory ${\sf D}_{L}$ of~${\mathcal{S}}^{\perp}$ formed by the objects of the form $L(X)$, for $X$ in~${\sf D}$, is a dense subcategory consisting of finitely presentable regular projectives.

To show that ${\sf D}_{L}$ is dense in ${\mathcal{S}}^{\perp}$, we must prove that the restricted Yoneda embedding ${\mathcal{S}}^{\perp} \to [{\sf D}_{L}^{{\mathrm{op}}},{\sf Set}]$ is fully faithful. That is, for every $Y_{1},Y_{2}$ in ${\mathcal{S}}^{\perp}$ the canonical map
\[
{\mathcal{S}}^{\perp}(Y_{1},Y_{2}) \to \mathrm{Nat}({\mathcal{S}}^{\perp}(-,Y_{1})_{\mid {\sf D}_{L}}, {\mathcal{S}}^{\perp}(-,Y_{2})_{\mid {\sf D}_{L}})
\]
is a bijection. Let $\tau$ be a natural transformation in the rightmost set above. The component of $\tau$ at any object $L(X)$ of ${\sf D}_{L}$ is 
\[
\tau_{L(X)}\colon {\mathcal{S}}^{\perp}(L(X),Y_{1})\to {\mathcal{S}}^{\perp}(L(X),Y_{2}),
\]
which, in view of the adjunction $L\dashv R$, yields a map
\[
{\sf C}(X, R(Y_{1}))\xrightarrow{\cong} {\mathcal{S}}^{\perp}(L(X),Y_{1}) \xrightarrow{\tau_{L(X)}} {\mathcal{S}}^{\perp}(L(X),Y_{2}) \xrightarrow{\cong} {\sf C}(X, R(Y_{2})).
\]
Let us denote the latter composite by $\sigma_{X}$. The naturality of $\tau$ entails that the maps~$\sigma_{X}$ are the components of a natural transformation 
\[
\sigma\colon {\sf C}(-,R(Y_{1}))_{\mid {\sf D}}\to {\sf C}(-,R(Y_{2}))_{\mid {\sf D}}.
\]
The restricted Yoneda embedding ${\sf C} \to [{\sf D}^{{\mathrm{op}}},{\sf Set}]$ is fully faithful because ${\sf D}$ is dense in ${\sf C}$. Hence, the natural transformation $\sigma$ is induced by a unique arrow $f\colon R(Y_{1})\to R(Y_{2})$. Since $R$ is the inclusion of a full subcategory, the arrow $f\colon Y_{1}\to Y_{2}$ lies in ${\mathcal{S}}^{\perp}$. Tracing $f$ through the adjunction, we see that it is the unique arrow inducing the natural transformation $\tau$. Therefore, ${\sf D}_{L}$ is dense in ${\mathcal{S}}^{\perp}$.

Now, the reflector $L$ preserves finitely presentable objects because $R$ preserves directed colimits; hence, each object in ${\sf D}_{L}$ is finitely presentable. To show that each object in ${\sf D}_{L}$ is regular projective, we start by proving the following fact.

\begin{claim}
The inclusion $R\colon {\mathcal{S}}^{\perp} \hookrightarrow {\sf C}$ preserves regular epimorphisms.
\end{claim}

\begin{proof}[Proof of Claim]
We first show that ${\mathcal{S}}^{\perp}$ is closed in ${\sf C}$ under regular images. Let $q\colon A\to B$ be a regular epimorphism in ${\sf C}$ with $A\in {\mathcal{S}}^{\perp}$. We must show that $B\in {\mathcal{S}}^{\perp}$, i.e.\ $B$ is orthogonal to each arrow $f\colon X \to Y$ in $\mathcal{S}$. If $g\colon X\to B$ is an arrow in ${\sf C}$, since $X$ is  regular projective there is $h\colon X\to A$ such that $g = q\circ h$.
 
\[\begin{tikzcd}
{} & A \arrow{d}{q} \\
X \arrow{r}{g} \arrow{d}[swap]{f} \arrow[dashed]{ur}{h} & B \\
Y \arrow[dashed]{ur}[swap]{\ell} & {}
\end{tikzcd}\]
Because $A\in {\mathcal{S}}^{\perp}$, there is $k\colon Y\to A$ such that $h = k\circ f$. Then $\ell\coloneqq q\circ k$ satisfies
\[
\ell \circ f = q\circ k \circ f = q\circ h = g,
\]
showing that $B\in {\mathcal{S}}^{\perp}$.

Next, we show that $R$ sends epimorphisms to regular epimorphisms, thus settling the claim. Let $e\colon X\to Y$ be an epimorphism in ${\mathcal{S}}^{\perp}$. Because every object of ${\sf C}$ admits a monomorphism to an object of ${\mathcal{S}}^{\perp}$, $R(e)$ is an epimorphism in ${\sf C}$. Since ${\sf C}$ is equivalent to a quasivariety, it admits a (regular epi, mono) factorisation system. Consider a decomposition of $R(e)$ as a regular epimorphism $q\colon R(X)\to A$ followed by a monomorphism $m\colon A\to R(Y)$. The object $A$ belongs to ${\mathcal{S}}^{\perp}$ because the latter is closed in ${\sf C}$ under regular images, and $m$ is an epi-mono because $R(e)$ is epi. Each object of ${\mathcal{S}}^{\perp}$ is saturated (e.g.\ by Proposition~\ref{p:saturated-Beth-comp-lfp}), therefore $m$ is an isomorphism. We conclude that $R(e)$ is a regular epimorphism.
\end{proof}


If $X$ is any object of ${\sf C}$, we have a natural isomorphism ${\mathcal{S}}^{\perp}(L(X),-)\cong {\sf C}(X,R(-))$. Since $R$ preserves regular epimorphisms by the previous claim, if $X$ is regular projective (i.e., if ${\sf C}(X,-)\colon {\sf C}\to{\sf Set}$ preserves regular epimorphisms) then so is $LX$. Thus, ${\sf D}_{L}$ consists of regular projective objects.

This shows that ${\mathcal{S}}^{\perp}$ is equivalent to a finitary quasivariety. Note that if ${\sf C}$ is equivalent to a mono-sorted finitary quasivariety, then we can choose the dense subcategory ${\sf D}$ to consist of a single object. The same proof as above then shows that ${\mathcal{S}}^{\perp}$ is equivalent to a mono-sorted finitary quasivariety.

It remains to show that if ${\sf C}$ is a variety, then so is ${\mathcal{S}}^{\perp}$. Recall that a quasivariety is a variety if, and only if, it has effective equivalence relations (cf.\ e.g.\ \cite[Corollary~3.25]{ar94book}). Therefore, we must prove that if equivalence relations in ${\sf C}$ are effective, the same holds in~${\mathcal{S}}^{\perp}$. Let $(r_{0},r_{1})\colon E\rightrightarrows X$ be an equivalence relation in~${\mathcal{S}}^{\perp}$. Because $R\colon {\mathcal{S}}^{\perp}\hookrightarrow {\sf C}$ preserves limits, $(R(r_{0}),R(r_{1}))$ is an equivalence relation in~${\sf C}$. As equivalence relations in the latter category are effective, $(R(r_{0}),R(r_{1}))$ is the kernel pair of its coequaliser $q\colon R(X)\to A$. The coequaliser of $(r_{0},r_{1})$ in ${\mathcal{S}}^{\perp}$ is the unique arrow $\tilde{q}\colon X\to L(A)$ such that $R(\tilde{q}) = \eta_{A}\circ q$, where $\eta_{A}\colon A \to RL(A)$ is the component at $A$ of the unit of the adjunction $L\dashv R$. Because $\eta_{A}$ is monic, the kernel pair of $\eta_{A}\circ q$ in ${\sf C}$ coincides with the kernel pair of $q$, hence with $(R(r_{0}),R(r_{1}))$. Since limits in ${\mathcal{S}}^{\perp}$ are computed in ${\sf C}$, it follows that the kernel pair of $\tilde{q}$ is $(r_{0},r_{1})$. We conclude that the latter equivalence relation is effective.

title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{p:transfer-AP}
Suppose that ${\sf C}$ satisfies the amalgamation property. Then $\mathcal{B}({\sf C})$ has the strong amalgamation property.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Since $\mathcal{B}({\sf C})$ is a reflective subcategory of ${\sf C}$, pushouts in the former category are computed by first taking the pushout in ${\sf C}$ and then applying the reflector. 
In view of \cite[Lemma~1]{Ringel1971}, given any full and replete mono-reflective subcategory of an lfp category that satisfies the amalgamation property, the reflector preserves monomorphisms. Hence, the reflector ${\sf C}\to\mathcal{B}({\sf C})$ preserves monos. The inclusion functor $\mathcal{B}({\sf C})\hookrightarrow{\sf C}$ preserves monos too, because it is right adjoint. Thus, since ${\sf C}$ satisfies \textnormal{AP}, so does $\mathcal{B}({\sf C})$. As \textnormal{ES}~and \textnormal{SES}~are equivalent in the presence of \textnormal{AP}, it follows that $\mathcal{B}({\sf C})$ satisfies \textnormal{SES}, and thus also \textnormal{SAP}~(cf.\ Proposition~\ref{l:IPA-iff-SES}).

title: Remark

title: Remark
body_md:
Let ${\sf DL}$ be the category of bounded distributive lattices and bounded lattice homomorphisms, and ${\sf BA}$ the full subcategory of ${\sf DL}$ consisting of Boolean algebras. The inclusion ${\sf BA}\hookrightarrow {\sf DL}$ has a left adjoint, which assigns to a distributive lattice its \emph{Boolean envelope}. A remarkable property of this adjunction is that, if we embed a distributive lattice $A$ into any Boolean algebra $B$, the Boolean subalgebra $\langle A\rangle$ of $B$ generated by (the image of) $A$ is isomorphic to the Booleanisation of $A$. Note that the inclusion $A\hookrightarrow \langle A\rangle$ is an epi-mono in ${\sf DL}$. 

Let us define the latter property for any reflective subcategory $R\colon \sf{E}\hookrightarrow {\sf D}$, with left adjoint $L$ and unit $\eta$. We shall say that such an adjunction has the \emph{free extension property} if, given any epi-mono $f\colon A\to R(X)$ in ${\sf D}$, the unique arrow $g\colon L(A)\to X$ such that the following diagram commutes is an isomorphism.
\[\begin{tikzcd}
A \arrow{r}{\eta_{A}} \arrow{dr}[swap]{f} & RL(A) \arrow{d}{R(g)} \\
{} & R(X)
\end{tikzcd}\]

It is a simple observation that, if ${\sf C}$ has the amalgamation property, the mono-reflective subcategory $\mathcal{B}({\sf C})\hookrightarrow{\sf C}$ has the free extension property. Just observe that, in any category satisfying \textnormal{AP}, epi-monos are \emph{essential monos} (recall that a mono~$m$ is an essential mono if any composite $h\circ m$ is monic just when $h$ is monic); for a proof, see \cite[\S 2]{Ringel1971}. It follows that the components $\eta_{A}$ of the unit are essential monos, and so $R(g)$ is epi-monic whenever $f$ is epi-monic. As $R$ reflects epis and monos because it is faithful, $g$ is an epi-mono in $\mathcal{B}({\sf C})$, hence an isomorphism.

We recover the free extension property for Boolean envelopes because ${\sf DL}$ satisfies the amalgamation property, and ${\sf BA}$ is the Beth companion of ${\sf DL}$ (cf.\ Section~\ref{s:examples}).

title: Remark
body_md:
The requirement for a monad to be strongly finitary is fairly restrictive. For instance, a monad on ${\sf Set}$ is strongly finitary if, and only if, its associated category of algebras is a finitary variety that is locally finite in the sense of universal algebra, meaning that any free algebra on a finite set is finite. 
 
Nevertheless, the monad $\mathbb{T}_\mathcal{X}$ is strongly finitary in several cases, including those of bounded distributive lattices and cancellative commutative monoids (cf.\ Section~\ref{s:examples}).

title: Remark
body_md:
Essentially algebraic logic has many different presentations. It was first introduced by Freyd under the name of \emph{Cartesian logic} \cite{Freyd1972AspectsOfTopoi,Freyd2002CartesianLogic}. Over the years, alternative approaches emphasising different syntactic elements have emerged. These include Cartmell's generalised algebraic theories \cite{Cartmell1986GeneralisedAlgebraicTheories}, and Palmgren and Vickers' partial Horn theories \cite{PalmgrenVickers2007PartialHorn}. 
These different presentations of the syntax are equiexpressive, and the corresponding syntactic categories are precisely the categories with finite limits. There are other categorical models of essentially algebraic theories. For example, \emph{clans} provide a more precise representation of generalised algebraic theories \cite{Frey2025DualityClans,ALN25}, while \emph{discrete Cartesian restriction categories} capture the partiality of some operations more faithfully \cite{DiLibertiEtAl2021PartialTheories}.

label: p:Beth-inverter
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{p:Beth-inverter}
  Let ${\sf C}$ be an lfp category satisfying \textnormal{EAP}, and suppose the monad~$\mathbb{T}_{\mathcal{X}}$ is strongly finitary. If ${\sf C}$ admits a Beth companion, then the latter is the inverter in ${\sf Lfp}$ of a set of epi-monos between finitely presentable objects of~${\sf C}$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
It follows from Remark~\ref{rmk:EAP-vs-TEM} and Theorem~\ref{thm:orthinverter} that there exists a set $\mathcal{H}$ of epi-monos between finitely presentable objects of ${\sf C}$ such that the Beth companion of ${\sf C}$ is the orthogonality class of $\mathcal{H}$.
 
We must show that the following diagram is an inverter in ${\sf Lfp}$.
\[
  \begin{tikzcd}
    {\mathcal{H}^\perp} &
    {\makebox[0.5cm][c]{${\sf C}$}}
    && {\makebox[0.5cm][c]{${\sf Set}^{\overline{\mathcal{H}}}$}}
    \arrow[hook, from=1-1, to=1-2]
    \arrow[""{name=2, anchor=center, inner sep=0},
      "{\mathsf{dom}(\mathcal{H})^*}",
      bend left=40, from=1-2, to=1-4]
    \arrow[""{name=3, anchor=center, inner sep=0},
      "{\mathsf{cod}(\mathcal{H})^*}"',
      bend right=40, from=1-2, to=1-4, shorten >=3pt]
    \arrow["{[\mathcal{H}]^*}"{description}, Rightarrow,
      from=3, to=2, shorten <=2pt, shorten >=2pt]
  \end{tikzcd}
\]


To this end, observe that the forgetful functor ${\sf Lfp} \to {\sf CAT}$ creates all $2$-limits, and in particular inverters, because it is $2$-conservative and preserves $2$-limits; for the latter fact, see \cite[Theorem~2.17]{Bird1984}. In turn, as mentioned above, the inverter in ${\sf CAT}$ is the full subcategory of ${\sf C}$ consisting of the objects $X$ such that, for each arrow $h\colon A \to B$ in $\mathcal{H}$, the induced map ${\sf C}(B,X) \to {\sf C}(A,X)$, $f \mapsto f \circ h$, is a bijection. This means precisely that ${\mathcal{H}}^{\perp}$ is the desired inverter.

title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{t:syntactic-Beth-companion}
  Let ${\sf C}$ be an lfp category satisfying \textnormal{EAP}, and suppose the monad~$\mathbb{T}_{\mathcal{X}}$ is strongly finitary. If the Beth companion $\mathcal{B}({\sf C})$ exists, its theory $\mathsf{Th}(\mathcal{B}({\sf C}))$ is the coinverter in ${\sf Lex}$ of a set of epi-monos in $\mathsf{Th}({\sf C})$.
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md: It is worth noting that the latter theorem is far from trivial, as the forgetful functor ${\sf Lex} \to {\sf Cat}$ does not preserve coinverters, and the description of coinverters in ${\sf Lex}$ is almost entirely formal. Indeed, ${\sf Lex}$ is $2$-monadic over ${\sf Cat}$, and colimits in categories of algebras are seldom computed in the underlying category, especially coequaliser-type colimits. Our proof relies crucially on Gabriel--Ulmer duality and on the fact that $2$-limits in ${\sf Lfp}$ are computed in ${\sf CAT}$.

label: p:CMon-no-Beth-companion
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{p:CMon-no-Beth-companion}
There is no balanced full mono-reflective subcategory of~${\sf CMon}$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let ${\sf D}\hookrightarrow {\sf CMon}$ be a balanced full mono-reflective subcategory, with unit $\eta$. We can assume without loss of generality that ${\sf D}$ is isomorphism-closed in ${\sf CMon}$. By Lemma~\ref{l:mono-refl-sat}, ${\sf D}$ contains all saturated monoids; in particular, it contains the monoids~$E_{n}$ defined above for every non-negative integer $n$, including $\mathbb{Z}$. 

Consider the component~$\eta_{\mathbb{N}}$ of the unit at $\mathbb{N}$. If $\eta_{\mathbb{N}}$ is an isomorphism, then $\mathbb{N}$ belongs to ${\sf D}$. But then the epi-monic inclusion $i\colon \mathbb{N}\hookrightarrow \mathbb{Z}$ belongs to ${\sf D}$, contradicting the fact that ${\sf D}$ is balanced.
 
On the other hand, if $\eta_{\mathbb{N}}$ is a proper epi-extension, it can be identified with the arrow ${\iota_{n}\colon \mathbb{N}\to E_{n}}$ that sends $1$ to $a$, for some $n$. Now, consider the unique arrow $\xi$ making the following diagram commute.
\[\begin{tikzcd}
\mathbb{N} \arrow{r}{\eta_{\mathbb{N}}} \arrow{dr}[swap]{\iota_{n+1}} & E_{n} \arrow{d}{\xi} \\
{} & E_{n+1}
\end{tikzcd}\]
If $q_{n}\colon E_{n+1}\twoheadrightarrow E_{n}$ is the natural quotient, the universal property of $\eta_{\mathbb{N}}$ implies that $q_{n}\circ \xi =\mathrm{id}_{E_{n}}$. This shows that $\xi$ is both a section and an epimorphism, hence an isomorphism. This is a contradiction.

label: p:CRng-no-Beth-companion
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{p:CRng-no-Beth-companion}
  The category ${\sf CRng}$ of commutative unital rings does not admit a Beth companion.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Suppose that ${\sf CRng}$ has a Beth companion. In this case, it coincides with its full subcategory of saturated rings by Theorem~\ref{t:Beth-companion-unique}. In view of \cite[Korollar~5.4, Korollar~6.3]{Storrer1968}, saturated rings include all fields and all finite cyclic rings~$\mathbb{Z}_n$.

Let $\eta_{\mathbb{Z}}\colon \mathbb{Z}\to R$ be the component at $\mathbb{Z}$ of the unit of the adjunction formed by the inclusion ${\sf Sat}({\sf CRng})\hookrightarrow {\sf CRng}$ and its left adjoint. Since $\mathbb{Z}$ is not saturated, the saturated ring $R$ is a proper epi-extension of $\mathbb{Z}$. We distinguish two cases, depending on whether $R$ has torsion.

If $R$ is torsion-free, then it is a solid ring of type~\ref{i:type-2}. But every subring of $\mathbb{Q}$ admits an epi-mono to $\mathbb{Q}$, so the only saturated solid ring of type~\ref{i:type-2} is $\mathbb{Q}$. The universal property of $R$ then implies that, for each prime $p$, there is an arrow $\mathbb{Q}\to \mathbb{F}_{p}$, which is a contradiction.

If $R$ has torsion, by \cite[Lemma~3.10]{BK1972} we have 
\begin{equation}\label{eq:solid-torsion}
  R^t\cong \bigoplus_{p\in K}{\mathbb{Z}_{p^{e(p)}}} \ \ \text{ and } \ \  R/R^t \cong \mathbb{Z}[J^{-1}]
\end{equation}
for some non-empty sets of primes $K\subseteq J$, and positive integers $e(p)$.\footnote{If $K$ is finite then $R$ is of type~\ref{i:type-3}; otherwise, $R$ is of type~\ref{i:type-4}.} Because $R$ is saturated, $J$ must be the set of all primes (just note that, if $q\notin J$, then $R\to R[q^{-1}]$ is a proper epi-mono), and so $R/R^t \cong \mathbb{Q}$. Consider any prime $p\in K$ and set $k\coloneqq e(p)+1$. Then the universal property of $R$ yields an arrow $f\colon R\to \mathbb{Z}_{p^k}$. We will show that this leads to a contradiction. Since $R/R^t \cong \mathbb{Q}$, $p$ is invertible modulo the torsion subgroup; that is, there are $x\in R$ and $t\in R^t$ such that $px=1+t$. The description of $R^t$ in eq.~\eqref{eq:solid-torsion} implies the existence of a finite set $\{q_1,\ldots,q_n\}\subseteq K \setminus\{p\}$ such that
\[
t = t_p + t_{q_1} + \dots + t_{q_n},
\]
with $t_p \in \mathbb{Z}_{p^{e(p)}}$ and $t_q \in \mathbb{Z}_{q^{e(q)}}$ for every $q\in \{q_1,\ldots,q_n\}$. Each such prime $q$ is invertible in $\mathbb{Z}_{p^k}$, and each $t_q$ is annihilated by some power of $q$, so $f(t_q)=0$. Hence, $f(t)= f(t_p)$. In particular,
\[
  p^{e(p)}\cdot f(t) = p^{e(p)}\cdot f(t_p) = f(p^{e(p)}t_p) = f(0) = 0.
\]
 
Therefore, the identity $px=1+t$ yields
\[
0 = p^k\cdot f(x) = p^{e(p)}(p\cdot f(x)) = p^{e(p)}(1 + f(t)) = p^{e(p)},
\]
which is false in $\mathbb{Z}_{p^k}$.

label: l:perfect-fields-balanced
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{l:perfect-fields-balanced}
The category ${\sf Field}_{\pi}$ of perfect fields is balanced.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: Every ring homomorphism between fields is injective. By Lemma~\ref{l:basic-props-mono-reflections}, epimorphisms in the category of perfect fields coincide with epimorphisms in the category of fields. Therefore, it suffices to show that every epimorphism in ${\sf Field}$ between perfect fields is surjective. In turn, it is well known that epimorphisms in ${\sf Field}$ are precisely the purely inseparable field extensions. Since perfect fields do not admit any non-trivial purely inseparable extension, every epimorphism in ${\sf Field}$ whose domain is a perfect field must be surjective.

label: l:lifting-p-annihilation
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{l:lifting-p-annihilation}
In any regular ring $A$, consider the element $e\coloneqq pp^{*}$, where $p$ denotes the sum of the unit $1$ with itself, $p$ times. For every $x\in A$, we have $p(1-e)x=0$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Computing the term $p(1-e)x$, we get
\[
p(1-e)x = (p-pe)x = (p-pp^{*}p)x=(p-p)x=0\cdot x =0.\qedhere
\]

title: Proposition
body_md: The category ${\sf RegRng}_{\pi}$ is balanced.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
As ${\sf RegRng}_{\pi}$ is an $\omega$-orthogonality class in ${\sf RegRng}$ associated with a set of epi-monos, and monos are pushout stable in ${\sf RegRng}$ \cite[Theorem~1.6]{Cornish1977}, it follows that ${\sf RegRng}_{\pi}$ is mono-reflective in ${\sf RegRng}$; cf.\ \cite[\S 1.37]{ar94book}. Thus, by Lemma~\ref{l:basic-props-mono-reflections}, every epi-mono in ${\sf RegRng}_{\pi}$ is epi-monic in ${\sf RegRng}$.

Recall from \cite[Theorem~10.3]{Pierce1967} that ${\sf RegRng}$ is dually equivalent to the category of regular ringed spaces. A \emph{regular ringed space} is a pair $(X, J)$ where $X$ is a Stone space and $J$ is a sheaf of fields on $X$. A \emph{morphism of regular ringed spaces} $(f,f^{\sharp})\colon (X,J)\to (Y,K)$ consists of a continuous map $f\colon X\to Y$ and a morphism $f^{\sharp}\colon K\to f_{*}J$ of sheaves of fields over $Y$, where $f_{*}$ denotes the direct image functor induced by $f$. Under this dual equivalence, the sheaf associated to a regular ring~$R$ is defined on the Stone space dual to the Boolean algebra of idempotents of $R$, whose points can be identified with the maximal ideals of $R$. The stalk of this sheaf at a maximal ideal $m$ is the field $R/m$.

Now let $h\colon R\to S$ be epi-monic in ${\sf RegRng}_{\pi}$. By the first paragraph, $h$ is epi-monic in ${\sf RegRng}$. We can identify $R$ with an epic subalgebra of $S$, and $h$ with the inclusion $R\hookrightarrow S$. Let $X_{R}$ and $X_{S}$ be the Stone spaces associated with $R$ and~$S$, respectively. We claim that the continuous map $X_{S}\to X_{R}$ induced by $h$ is a homeomorphism; that is, for every maximal ideal~$m$ of $R$ there is a unique maximal ideal $n$ of~$S$ such that $n\cap R = m$. 
 
To see that such a maximal ideal $n$ exists, it suffices to prove that the ideal $\overline{m}$ of $S$ generated by~$m$ is proper, for then it can be extended to a maximal ideal $n$ satisfying $n\cap R \supseteq m$, and so $n\cap R = m$ by maximality of~$m$. Suppose that $1\in \overline{m}$, i.e., $1=\sum{a_{i}b_{i}}$ for finitely many elements $a_{i}\in m$ and $b_{i}\in S$. Let $I\subseteq R$ be the ideal generated by the~$a_{i}$'s. In a regular ring, every finitely generated ideal is principal and is generated by an idempotent element \cite[Theorem~1.1]{Goodearl1991}. If $e\in R$ is an idempotent element that generates $I$, then $ex=x$ for every $x\in I$. Therefore,
\[
1 =\textstyle\sum{a_{i}b_{i}} = \sum{(ea_{i})b_{i}} = e\sum{a_{i}b_{i}} = e\cdot 1 = e
\]
and so $1\in I \subseteq m$, contradicting the fact that $m$ is maximal. Hence, $\overline{m}$ is proper. 

Next, assume $n_{1},n_{2}$ are maximal ideals of $S$ satisfying $n_{1}\cap R = m = n_{2}\cap R$. 
Then $L_{1}\coloneqq S/n_{1}$ and $L_{2}\coloneqq S/n_{2}$ are field extensions of $K\coloneqq R/m$. Since ${\sf Field}$ has the amalgamation property, there is a field $F$ such that the span of field extensions $L_{1}\hookleftarrow K \hookrightarrow L_{2}$ can be completed to a commutative diagram as displayed below.
\[\begin{tikzcd}[row sep=1em, column sep=1em]
{} & L_{1} \arrow[hookrightarrow]{dr} & \\
K \arrow[hookrightarrow]{ur} \arrow[hookrightarrow]{dr} & & F \\
{} & L_{2} \arrow[hookrightarrow]{ur} &
\end{tikzcd}\]
Define the arrows $g_{1}\colon S\to L_{1}\hookrightarrow F$ and $g_{2}\colon S\to L_{2}\hookrightarrow F$ in ${\sf RegRng}$, where the first morphisms in the two composites are the quotient maps. 
The restrictions of $g_{1}$ and~$g_{2}$ to~$R$ coincide, however, if $n_{1}\neq n_{2}$ there exists $x\in n_{1}\setminus n_{2}$ and so $g_{1}(x) = 0$ while $g_{2}(x)\neq 0$. As the inclusion $R\hookrightarrow S$ is epic, we conclude that $n_{1}=n_{2}$. 

For each maximal ideal $n$ of $S$, write $m\coloneqq n\cap R$. The induced field homomorphism $R/m\to S/n$ is monic. It is also epic in ${\sf Field}$: if $u,v\colon S/n\rightrightarrows F$ agree on $R/m$, then the composites $S\to S/n\rightrightarrows F$ agree on $R$, and therefore coincide because $R\hookrightarrow S$ is epic. Thus, each stalk map of the Pierce sheaves is epi-monic in ${\sf Field}$. Since $R$ and~$S$ are perfect, each residue field is perfect, so Lemma~\ref{l:perfect-fields-balanced} yields that every stalk map is an isomorphism. Identifying $X_{S}$ with $X_{R}$ via the homeomorphism established above, we obtain a stalkwise isomorphism of sheaves of fields on the same Stone space, hence an isomorphism of Pierce sheaves. Therefore, $h$ is an isomorphism in ${\sf RegRng}$, and a fortiori in ${\sf RegRng}_{\pi}$.

label: l:monoreflection-coslices
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Recall that, for any lfp category $\sf E$ and any object $e$ of $\sf E$, the coslice $e/{\sf E}$ is also lfp \cite[Proposition~1.57]{ar94book}. Moreover, the forgetful functor $e/{\sf E}\to {\sf E}$ creates limits and connected colimits (see e.g.\ \cite[Proposition~3.3.8]{Riehl2016book}). In particular, it creates monomorphisms, directed colimits and pushouts.

\ref{i:coslice-adj} Denote by $\eta$ the unit of the adjunction formed by the inclusion ${\sf C} \hookrightarrow {\sf D}$ and its left adjoint. The inclusion $c/{\sf C} \hookrightarrow c/{\sf D}$ admits a left adjoint that sends an object $f\colon c\to A$ to the composite $\eta_{A} \circ f$. The unit at~$f$ of the latter reflection is $\eta_{A}$, regarded as an arrow in $c/{\sf D}$. Since $\eta_{A}$ is monic in ${\sf D}$ and the forgetful functor $c/{\sf D}\to {\sf D}$ creates monomorphisms, it follows that $c/{\sf C}$ is mono-reflective in $c/{\sf D}$. Moreover, the inclusion $c/{\sf C}\hookrightarrow c/{\sf D}$ preserves directed colimits because ${\sf C}\hookrightarrow {\sf D}$ does, and directed colimits are a particular type of connected colimits.

\ref{i:coslice-TM} Suppose that ${\sf C}$ has transferable monos. Equivalently, monomorphisms in~${\sf C}$ are stable under all pushouts. Because the forgetful functor $c/{\sf C}\to {\sf C}$ creates monomorphisms and pushouts, we conclude that $c/{\sf C}$ has transferable monos.

title: Proposition
body_md: If $k$ has characteristic $0$, then $k/{\sf RegRng}$ is balanced.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Observe that $k/{\sf RegRng}$ is a reflective subcategory of $k/{\sf CRng}$, although not a mono-reflective one. This follows from the proof of Lemma~\ref{l:monoreflection-coslices}, recalling that ${\sf RegRng}$ is a reflective subcategory of ${\sf CRng}$ (and even an $\omega$-orthogonality class in~${\sf CRng}$). In particular, the inclusion $k/{\sf RegRng}\hookrightarrow k/{\sf CRng}$ preserves monomorphisms. If we show that it sends epis to surjections, it will follow that it sends epi-monos to isomorphisms, and therefore $k/{\sf RegRng}$ is balanced.

Let $f\colon A \to B$ be an epimorphism in $k/{\sf RegRng}$. The cokernel pair of $f$ is given by taking the pushout of $f$ along itself in $k/{\sf CRng}$, which yields the tensor product $R\coloneqq B\otimes_{A} B$, and then applying the left adjoint to the inclusion $k/{\sf RegRng} \hookrightarrow k/{\sf CRng}$. Write $\nu(R)$ for the resulting regular $k$-algebra, and let $\eta\colon R \to \nu(R)$ be the reflection morphism. The kernel of $\eta$ is the nilradical of $R$ (as can be seen by factoring $k/{\sf RegRng} \hookrightarrow k/{\sf CRng}$ via the mono-reflective subcategory $k/{\sf RegRng} \hookrightarrow k/{\sf RedRng}$). 

We claim that $R$ is reduced, and so $\eta$ is injective. It is enough to show that $R$ embeds in a product of reduced rings. Recall that the canonical map from any $A$-module to the product of its localisations at the maximal ideals of $A$ is injective. In particular, there is an injective homomorphism
\[
R \hookrightarrow \prod_{m\in \mathrm{Max}(A)}{R_{m}}
\] 
where $\mathrm{Max}(A)$ is the set of maximal ideals of $A$, and $R_{m}$ is the localisation of $R$ at~$A\setminus m$. It suffices to prove that each $R_{m}$ is reduced. Localisations commute with tensor products, hence we get
\[
R_{m} = (B\otimes_{A} B)_{m} \cong B_{m} \otimes_{A_{m}} B_{m}.
\]
Since $A$ is regular, the localisation $A_{m}$ is a field (see e.g.\ \cite[Theorem~1.16]{Goodearl1991}), and so it is a field extension of $k$. Because $k$ has characteristic $0$, so does $A_{m}$; in particular, $A_{m}$ is a perfect field.
 
Moreover, regular rings are closed under localisations. Just observe that, if $C$ is a regular ring and $S\subseteq C$ is a multiplicative subset, then for each element $x=\frac{a}{s}\in S^{-1}C$, there exists $b\in C$ such that $a=a^{2}b$. The element $y\coloneqq sb$ then satisfies
\[
x = \frac{a}{s} = \frac{a^{2}b}{s} = \bigg(\frac{a}{s}\bigg)^{2} (sb) = x^{2} y,
\]
showing that $S^{-1}C$ is regular. Therefore, $B_{m}$ is a regular ring and, in particular, reduced. For any perfect field $K$, the tensor product of reduced $K$-algebras is reduced (see e.g.\ \cite[Ch.~V, \S 15, Th\'eor\`eme~3]{BourbakiAlgebra4-7}). Therefore, $R_{m}$ is reduced. 

Now, consider the cokernel pair of $f$ in $k/{\sf CRng}$, as displayed below.
\[\begin{tikzcd}
B \arrow[yshift=3pt]{r}{c_{0}} \arrow[yshift=-3pt]{r}[swap]{c_{1}} & R
\end{tikzcd}\]
The cokernel pair of $f$ in $k/{\sf RegRng}$ is $(\eta\circ c_{0},\eta\circ c_{1})$. As $f$ is epic in $k/{\sf RegRng}$, we get $\eta\circ c_{0} = \eta\circ c_{1}$, and thus $c_{0}=c_{1}$ because $\eta$ is injective. That is, $f$ is an epimorphism in $k/{\sf CRng}$. Viewing epimorphisms as connected colimits, it follows that~$f$ is an epimorphism in ${\sf CRng}$. In turn, every epimorphism in ${\sf CRng}$ whose domain is regular is a surjection; see e.g.\ \cite[Theorems~2.1 and~3.12]{Tarizadeh2022}.
